Carbon Capture Hot Paper
Oxygen-Assisted Supercapacitive Swing Adsorption of Carbon Dioxide
Muhammad Bilal, Jiajie Li, Neelesh Kumar, Bar Mosevitzky, Israel E. Wachs, and Kai Landskron*
Abstract: We report on the supercapacitive swing adsorption (SSA) of carbon dioxide at different voltage windows in the presence of oxygen using activated carbon electrodes, and deliquescent, aqueous electrolytes. The presence of O2 in the CO2/N2 gas mixture results in an up to 11 times higher CO2 adsorption capacity with 3 M MgBr2 (at 0.6 V) and up to 4–5 times higher adsorption capacity with 3 M MgCl2 (at 1 V). A tradeoff between high CO2 adsorption capacities and lower coulombic efficiencies was observed at voltages above 0.6 V. The energetic and adsorptive performance of the electrodes in the presence of oxygen below 0.5 V was similar to the performance with a CO2/N2 mixture without oxygen at 1 V. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of the electrodes demonstrate that the specific capacitance increases while the diffusion resistance decreases in the presence of oxygen. Oxygen concentrations ranging between 5–20 % give similar energetic and adsorptive performance. The electrodes exhibit stable performance for up to 100 cycles of operation.
Introduction
Electrochemical CO2 capture and concentration has emerged as a potentially safer, more energy efficient, modular and scalable alternative to traditional thermochemical methods which tend to be energy-intensive, and frequently use toxic and corrosive chemicals such as amines
and hydroxides. Unlike thermochemical methods, electrochemical methods can be carried out isothermally, avoiding the energy penalty associated with temperature changes.[1–4] Most electrochemical capture methods are based on redox reactions, that capture CO2 through either electrochemical modulation of proton concentration (pH swing),[5,6] electrochemical generation of nucleophiles by reducing redoxactive organic molecules,[7–9] or electrochemically mediated amine regeneration (EMAR).[10–12] The current challenges with redox-based techniques revolve around oxygen sensitivity, high materials cost, cycle stability, and energy losses due the overpotentials associated with the redox process.[13] The presence of oxygen significantly lowers the coulombic/ energy efficiencies by either deactivating the redox active compound or by directly participating in redox reactions. Supercapacitive techniques are attractive alternatives to redox-based techniques, and can be divided into membrane capacitive deionization (MCDI), and supercapacitive swing adsorption (SSA).[14,15] In contrast to redox-based techniques, the potential window is continuously variable, and the methods are based on inexpensive, non-toxic activated carbon materials and aqueous solutions. Moreover, supercapacitors are known for high round-trip energy efficiency and cycle stability, offering potential advantages pertaining to energy consumption and system lifetime. Compared to MCDI, SSA does not require membranes, and the gas mixture is fed directly through the SSA module, whereas in MCDI, the gas is first dissolved in water and then fed through the MCDI module. Since the first report on SSA by our group, significant technological progress has been made towards improving the cell design, increasing the CO2 adsorption capacity, and demonstrating the scalability potential through bipolar electrode stacks.[16–18] Fundamental studies on SSA focused on the acquisition of energetics and adsorptive performance metrics as a function of charging protocols, electrolyte composition, and concentration.[19–21] Recent studies highlighted the potential for enhancing CO2 sorption capacity by tuning the voltage window, investigated critical factors contributing towards performance improvements, and proposed biomass- and non-biomass derived carbon-based materials with high surface areas and capacitances for enhancing SSA performance.[17,22–24] To date, a maximum CO2 sorption capacity of ~ 520 mmol kg 1 at an energy consumption of ~ 130 kJ mol 1 is reported with 15 % CO2/ 85 % N2 gas mixtures.[24] Recently, Forse et el. Reported the supercapacitive swing adsorption of pure O2, and 20 % CO2/ 15 % O2/ 65 % N2 gas mixtures.[22] Partially reversible O2

adsorption was measured in experiments with pure O2 when the negative electrode was the gas-exposed electrode, but the amounts were not quantified. No significant O2 adsorption was measured with the positive electrode as the gasexposed electrode. Energy consumptions as low as 0.3 kJ mol 1 were reported with the positive electrode as the gas-exposed electrode, and the adsorption rates were as high as 300 mmol kg 1 h 1 (83 μmol kg 1 s 1) for the gas mixture. However, the investigations were performed in closed adsorption cells using pressure changes and did not allow for actual gas separation. No data was provided for the adsorptive and energetic performance of the CO2/N2/O2 mixtures with the negative electrode as the gas-exposed electrode.[22] Here, we report that oxygen assists the supercapacitive swing adsorption of carbon dioxide when the negative electrode is the gas-exposed electrode, leading to adsorption capacities that are up to 11 times enhanced. All experiments were performed in batch-mode under continuous gas flow allowing for actual gas separation. In our study, we used gas mixtures containing 15 % CO2 and 5–20 % O2 balanced with N2. Coal-derived BPL 4x6 carbon (Calgon) and garlic rootsderived micro-mesoporous carbon were used as electrode materials, and two different aqueous solutions (3 M MgBr2, 3 M MgCl2) were used as deliquescent electrolytes. Deliquescent electrolytes avoid water evaporation under continuous gas flow at relative humidity ranges typical for air (20100 %) and flue gases (close to 100 %). We further present strategies for improving the energy efficiency in the presence of oxygen. Scheme 1 shows the experimental setup and the individual components of the SSA cell. Further details are presented in the experimental section..
Results and Discussion
Figure 1 shows the voltage changes and CO2 concentration profiles during charging and discharging of an SSA module with 3 M MgBr2 as the electrolyte and 4x6 BPL carbon as
electrode material. When a 15 % CO2/85 % N2 gas mixture is flown through the SSA module, the CO2 concentration decreases during charging from 0 V to 1 V and goes back to the equilibrium concentration during the 20 min voltage holding step at 1 V (Figure 1a). The CO2 concentration increases upon discharging the module from 1 V to 0 V and reaches the equilibrium concentration during the 20 min voltage holding step at 0 V. The voltage curves are linear, and the adsorption/desorption is reversible. As the gas mixture is replaced with 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2, a large deviation from the linear behavior of voltage change is observed, and charging/discharging cycles and CO2 concentration changes are no longer reversible (Figure 1b). A much larger change in CO2 concentration is observed. The non-linear behavior of the voltage curves beyond 0.8 V and below 0.2 V is attributed to the onset of faradaic reactions due to the presence of oxygen.[25] To avoid these faradaic reactions and improve the reversibility of CO2 adsorption and desorption during SSA experiments with oxygen, the voltage window was reduced from 1 V to 0.6 V (between 0.2 to 0.8 V). Lowering the voltage window led to nearly linear charge–discharge curves indicating capacitive-like behavior, and reversible CO2 adsorption and desorption, respectively (Figure 1c). However, the CO2 concentration curves did not fully return to the original value (15 %) despite the much longer voltage holding times of 90 min, indicating that the equilibrium sorption capacity has not been reached yet. Further lowering of the voltage window from 0.6 to 0.4 V led to CO2 concentration curves that achieved their equilibrium adsorption capacity during the first 20 minutes of voltage holding step (Figure 1d), similar to the CO2/N2 gas mixture without oxygen. The energetic and adsorptive performance of SSA with 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2 gas mixture at 1 V, 0.6 V, and 0.4 V was compared with 15 % CO2/85 % N2 gas mixture at 1 V (Figure 2 and Table S1). In the absence of oxygen, a capacitance value of 90 F g 1 and resistance of 8 Ω cm2 resulted in CO2 adsorption capacity of ~ 65 mmol kg 1 at an adsorption rate of ~ 40 μmol kg 1 s 1 (Figure 2a and 2b).
Scheme 1. Supercapacitive swing adsorption (SSA) experimental setup. The gas mixture enters the mass flow controller, then passes through a bubbler filled with electrolyte which moistens the gas and enters the SSA cell through the center inlet port. The gas flows radially through the SSA cell, exits from the side outlet port, passes through a drying tube, and enters the CO2/O2 detector. The images are not according to scale. W/WS and C/R stands for working, working sense, counter, and reference electrode.

High coulombic efficiency (~ 97 %) and energy efficiency (~ 80 %) was achieved during cyclic charging, voltage holding after charging, discharging, and voltage holding after discharging (Figure 2c). Both charging and discharging capacitance values are similar (Table S1), and the less than 100 % of energy efficiency is due to the energy loss from the voltage holding after the charging step. An energy loss of 4 J and a sorption capacity of 65 mmol kg 1 resulted in an energy consumption value of ~ 80 kJ mol 1 (Figure 2d). In the presence of 5 % oxygen, a large deviation from capacitive to faradaic behavior of the electrodes at 1 V resulted in high resistance, very large charge storage capacity, and low coulombic and energy efficiency values (Figure 1b and Table S1). Although a higher CO2 adsorption capacity of 1590 mmol kg 1 was calculated for the first 3 SSA cycles, the continuously declining and irreversible performance of the electrodes along with large energy loss and energy consumption values restricted the use of the 1 V voltage window in the presence of oxygen. Lowering the voltage window to 0.6 V (from 0.2 to 0.8 V) restored the capacitive-like behavior of the electrodes as seen in Fig
ure 1c. A capacitance value of ~ 250 F g 1 (discharge capacitance value of 154 F g 1, Table S1) and a resistance of ~ 9 Ω cm2 at 0.6 V resulted in a CO2 adsorption capacity of ~ 750 mmol kg 1 and an adsorption rate of 120 μmol kg 1 s 1 at an energy consumption of ~ 300 kJ mol 1. This is ~ 11 times higher than the adsorption capacity calculated without oxygen in the gas mixture at 1 V. It should be noted that this amount is still not an equilibrium amount because the concentration curves did not return to 15 % despite the much longer potential holding times, showing that CO2 was still appreciably adsorbed at the end of the potential holding step. For this reason, the reversibility of the adsorption could not be accurately determined. The desorption begins at a CO2 concentration < 15 % which creates uncertainties pertaining to the size of the desorption integral. Assuming integrals as shown in Figure S1b and S1c, the ratio of moles of CO2 adsorbed to desorbed is between 1 (595 μmol CO2 captured during the charging step and 593 μmol CO2 released during the discharging step, Table S1) as the upper limit and 0.26 (158 μmol desorbed CO2) as the lower limit. The lower limit corresponds 195 mmol kg-1 of CO2 desorp

Sequentially charging and discharging of the electrodes within a voltage window of 0.6 V resulted in reproducible CO2 adsorption and desorption behavior which was not possible at 1 V (Figure S1a). However, a large energy loss (~ 190 J) and higher leakage
currents resulted in poor coulombic efficiency (~ 33 %) and energy efficiency (~ 8 %) values even at lower voltage window of 0.6 V. Further lowering the voltage window to 0.4 V ( 0.2 to 0.6 V) resulted in reduced capacitance (~ 90 F g 1), reduced adsorption capacity (~ 66 mmol kg 1) and adsorption rate

(~ 38 μmol kg 1
.s 1), higher coulombic efficiency (~ 88 %) and energy efficiency (~ 67 %), and lower energy loss (~ 4.6 J) and energy consumption (85 kJ mol 1) values (Figure 2a–d). The energetic and adsorptive performance of the electrodes with 5 % oxygen at 0.4 V ( 0.2 V to 0.6 V) is similar to the performance with CO2/N2 mixture without oxygen at 1 V. Cycling the electrodes for over 100 chargedischarge cycles at 0.4 V in the presence of 5 % oxygen resulted in nearly similar coulombic/energy efficiency, and adsorption capacity values, signifying oxygen stability (Figure 2e and Table S2). These results suggest that faradaic reactions due to oxygen fade away at reduced voltages, and oxygen assists in CO2 adsorption even at lower voltages. Switching the gas mixture from 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2 back to 15 % CO2/85 % N2 without oxygen and cycling at 1 V resulted in high capacitance and high adsorption capacity values to 210 F g 1 and 175 mmol kg 1, but the coulombic and energy efficiency values stayed low (39 % and 12 %, respectively, Figure S2), indicating irreversible changes in the electrodes during cycling with oxygen. Further experiments showing the irreversible O2 adsorption at voltages > 0.6 V, causing permanent changes to the electrodes are shown in the later section of the paper. The influence of oxygen on the charge storage behavior during SSA tests was investigated by cyclic voltammetry (CV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), Figure 3. Without oxygen, a quasi-rectangular shaped CV was obtained during charging and discharging of the supercapacitor from 0 to 1 V, referring to the double-layer capacitive type charge storage (red curve in Figure 3a). With oxygen, the CV curve somewhat deviates from the rectangular shaped behavior and shows increasing currents at voltages above 0.6 V and below 0.2 V (black curve). When the voltage window was reduced between 0.2 to 0.6 V, the capacitive behavior was restored (blue curve). These results argue that the presence of O2 in the gas mixture lowers the electrochemical capacitive window of carbon electrodes. Nyquist plots from EIS data showed a slight increase in solution resistance, a slight decrease in diffusion resistance, deviation from the quasi-vertical behavior at low frequencies, and smaller imaginary impedance in
the presence of 5 % oxygen (Figure 3b). The capacitance increases from ~ 90 F/g to ~ 150 F/g when O2 is present in the gas mixture (Figure 3c), suggesting partially reversible charge-transfer between the electrodes and adsorbed O2.[26] In situ spectroscopic analysis beyond the scope of this work is needed to clarify the chemical processes at the electrodes, and these investigations are on the way in our laboratory. The lower diffusion resistance and larger capacitance from EIS plots suggest improved pore accessibility and increased pore wettability enhancing specific capacitance in the presence of O2.[26–30] Overall, SSA experiments with 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2 gas mixture using 3 M MgBr2 attained a record adsorption capacity of ~ 750 mmol kg 1 at an energy consumption of ~ 300 kJ mol 1 at 0.6 V, while low energy consumption of 85 kJ mol 1 with a reversible adsorption capacity of ~ 66 mmol kg 1 was achieved at 0.4 V. The influence of oxygen on CO2 adsorption was further investigated with 3 M MgCl2 (Figure 4 and Figure S3), another deliquescent electrolyte. When a 15 % CO2/85 % N2 gas mixture is used, CO2 sorption profiles during charging and discharging behave very similarly to those shown by electrodes infiltrated with 3 M MgBr2 electrolyte (Figure 4a and Figure 1a). A capacitance of ~ 80 F g 1, a resistance of ~ 9 Ω cm2, a CO2 adsorption capacity of 75 mmol kg 1, an adsorption rate of ~ 32 μmol kg 1 s 1, a coulombic efficiency of ~ 98 %, an energy efficiency of ~ 80 %, an energy loss of ~ 4 J and an energy consumption of ~ 73 kJ mol 1 were measured (Figure 4c–f). These numbers are similar to the results obtained with 3 M MgBr2. The presence of 5 % O2 in the gas mixture resulted in much enhanced CO2 sorption (Figure 4b). Unlike 3 M MgBr2, the use of 3 M MgCl2 electrolyte in the presence of oxygen allowed the use of a 1 V voltage window with repeatable charging/discharging and CO2 sorption profiles. This shows that Br becomes reactive at 1 V in the presence of O2, while Cl does not. A capacitance value of ~ 109 F g 1 and a sorption capacity of 320 mmol kg 1 was obtained, four times higher than without oxygen (Figure 4c–d). Unlike for 3 M MgBr2, the CO2 concentration returned close to the 15 % value at the end of the potential holding step. The ratio of adsorbed to desorbed CO2 is between 0.86 and 1.23,
Figure 3. Influence of oxygen on the electrochemical performance of the supercapacitor under CO2/O2/N2 gas flow, showing: (a) CV curves at 1 V without O2 (shown in red), 1 V with 5 % O2 (shown in black) and 0.4 V with 5 % O2 (shown in blue) acquired using a scan rate of 5 mV s 1, (b) Nyquist plots from EIS data showing changes in solution resistance (Rs) and diffusion resistance (Rd) in the presence of O2 and (c) capacitance changes at different frequencies with and without O2.

compared to 0.89 without O2 at 1 V (Figure S4). Values smaller than 1 (0.86 and 0.89) may be attributed to CO2 formation due to minor oxidation of the carbon electrodes.[17] To investigate the possibility of increased CO2 adsorption at higher voltages, the voltage window was increased from 1 V to 1.2 V. However, the GCD curve irreversibly deviated from the capacitive to faradaic behavior beyond 1 V, suggesting that at voltages above 1 V also Cl becomes reactive in the presence of O2. (Figure S3e). Possibly, H2O2 diffuses from the negative to the positive electrode where it irreversibly oxidizes chloride ions in the double layer. The same mechanism may also explain the
irreversible behavior of the bromide electrolyte at 1 V. The different on-set voltage for Br and Cl degradation may be attributed to the more facile oxidation of Br relative to Cl . More studies beyond the scope of this work are needed to unambiguously answer these questions. The coulombic efficiency, energy efficiency, and energy consumption at 1 V is 60 %, 22 %, and 300 kJ mol 1 CO2, respectively (Figure 4e–f). The low energy efficiency and higher energy consumption values in the presence of oxygen were attributed to the much longer voltage holding times (30 min without O2 vs 90 min with O2) required to achieve equilibrium CO2 sorption and longer charging times (11 min
Figure 4. Voltage vs CO2 sorption profiles and corresponding energetic and adsorptive performance metrics of SSA with BPL electrodes and a 3 M MgCl2 electrolyte, showing: voltage and CO2 concentration at 1 V with a (a) 15 % CO2/85 % N2 gas mixture and (b) a 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2 gas mixture, (c) capacitance and resistance, (d) CO2 adsorption capacity and adsorption rate, (e) coulombic efficiency and energy efficiency and (f) energy loss and energy consumption at 1 V without O2, and at 1 V, 0.6 V and 0.4 V with 5 % O2.

without O2 vs 15 min with O2) due to the higher capacitance. To reduce the energy consumption of SSA in the presence of oxygen, additional experiments were performed by setting the voltage window between 0.2 to 0.8 V and between 0 to 0.5 V (Figure S3c–d). The smallest energy consumption in the presence of 5 % O2 (88 kJ.mol 1 CO2) was obtained at 0.5 V, with other energetics and adsorptive performance metrics approaching the performance metrics obtained with CO2/N2 mixture without oxygen at 1 V (Figure 4c–f). The reduced energy consumption, higher energy efficiency, and capacitive behavior of the electrodes at lower voltage-window was further confirmed from the quasirectangular CV curve at 0.5 V compared to the CV curves at 0.6 V and 1 V (Figure S3f). Overall, the electrodes infiltrated with 3 M MgCl2 electrolyte allowed the use of a voltage window up to 1 V in the presence of oxygen, and a tradeoff between higher adsorption capacity and lower energy efficiency was observed. Overall, the adsorption capacities measured with Br as electrolyte are significantly higher compared to Cl-. Possibly, bromide reacts with peroxosurface functionalities, and H2O2 formed at the negative electrode to produce hypobromide (OBr ) and H2O. Hypobromide is a weak base, which may further increase the pH near the negative electrode leading to more CO2 adsorption. We also investigated the possibility of irreversible O2 sorption to the electrodes at different voltages by simultaneously measuring the voltage changes, O2 concentration changes, and CO2 concentration changes. With 3 M MgBr2, 1950 μmol of O2 were irreversibly added to the carbon electrodes at 1 V voltage window, and the charging curve deviated from the capacitive behavior (Figure S5a). At 0.6 V, an average of 110 μmol O2 ware irreversibly sorbed during each charging step without any noticeable O2 desorption during the discharging step. At 0.4 V, ~ 4 μmol ware irreversibly sorbed (Figure S5b and S5c). With 3 M MgCl2, an average of 213 μmol O2 were irreversibly sorbed during each charging sequence at 1 V, 52 μmol were sorbed at 0.8 V, 9 μmol were sorbed at 0.6 V (Figure S6a–c). At 0.4 V, the O2 sorption become very small and noticeably reversible (Figure S6d). Charging to 0.4 V leads to CO2 adsorption and O2 desorption while a discharging cycle leads to CO2 desorption and O2 adsorption. The smaller and reversible O2 sorption restores the coulombic energy efficiency values at voltages less than 0.5 V. Both CO2 sorption and O2 sorption are significantly higher for MgBr2 compared to MgCl2 (Figure S5 and S6). The results agree with previous results in which MgCl2 infiltrated electrodes provided significantly improved coulombic and energy efficiency values compared to MgBr2 infiltrated electrodes. These results suggest that minimizing the voltage window to less than 0.5 V or increasing the electrodes overpotential towards irreversible O2 sorption (through possible oxygen reduction reaction) is critical for high coulombic/energy efficiency and long-term stability of the electrodes in an O2 environment. The energetic and sorptive performance of SSA was further investigated with garlic roots derived activated carbon and MgCl2 electrolyte. Garlic roots derived activated carbon showed a micro-mesoporous type N2 sorption
isotherm (Figure S7). The voltage changes and CO2 sorption profiles during charging and discharging exhibit a reversible and reproducible behavior at different voltage windows (Figure S8). The capacitance increases from ~ 135 F g 1 to ~ 250 F g 1 while the sorption capacity increases remarkably from 150 mmol kg 1 to 780 mmol kg 1 at 1 V as the gas mixture is switched from 15 % CO2/85 % N2 to 15 % CO2/ 5 % O2 80 % N2 (Figure 5a). The upper and the lower limits for the ratio of adsorbed to desorbed CO2 are 0.98 and 1.49 respectively, signifying that most of the adsorption is reversible. Around 85 % increase in capacitance is accompanied with 460 % increase in CO2 adsorption capacity in the presence of 5 % O2. These findings are in line with previously obtained results from BPL carbon where the capacitance increased 40 % and CO2 adsorption capacity increased 320 % when 5 % O2 was used in the gas mixture. Nonetheless, an adsorption capacity of ~ 780 mmol kg 1 obtained at an energy consumption of ~ 220 kJ mol 1 approaches the benchmarks set in conventional amine-based CO2 capture methods.[9] Table S6 shows a performance comparison of SSA with previous SSA studies and other recent electrochemical CO2 capture methods. Despite the higher adsorption capacity and reduced energy consumption with garlic roots-derived electrodes, the average coulombic efficiency of SSA charging and discharging cycles at 1 V stayed around 60 % when O2 is used in the gas mixture (Figure 5a). To improve the coulombic efficiency and energy consumption by minimizing the voltage holding time, the voltage and CO2 concentration curve in Figure S8b was analyzed for 0 min, 30 min, and 60 min of holding after charging (Table S4). The coulombic efficiency improved to ~ 84 %, and an adsorption capacity of ~ 350 mmol kg 1 at an energy consumption of 130 kJ mol 1 is obtained at 0 min of voltage hold, signifying the need to minimize the voltage holding times via the enhancement of adsorption rates. Minimizing the voltage window from 1 V to 0.6, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3 V also improved the coulombic efficiency to as high as 99 % (at 0.3 V) and energy consumption to as low as 35 kJ mol 1 (at 0.3 V), but at smaller sorption capacity of ~ 40 mmol kg 1 (Figure 5a). In order to understand the influence of the oxygen concentration, we performed additional experiments at 10, 15, and 20 % O2 while keeping the CO2 concentration constant at 15 %. Oxygen concentration ranging from 10 to 20 % give similar energetic and adsorptive performance (Figure S9 and Table S5), showing the insensitivity of SSA to variable oxygen concentrations. The adsorption of CO2 relative to O2 was investigated at a voltage window of 0.5 V (Figure 5b). On the same concentration scale, the changes in O2 concentration relative to the changes in CO2 concentration are barely noticeable (only 0.05 % change for O2 compared to ~ 1.5 % for CO2). Zooming in the O2 concentration curves shows that while a charging cycle corresponds to CO2 adsorption and a discharging cycle corresponds to CO2 desorption, initial desorption followed by adsorption of O2 was measured during charging. During discharging, fast adsorption followed by slower adsorption of O2 is observed. The average
Angewandte Chemie

Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202404881 (7 of 11) © 2024 The Author(s). Angewandte Chemie International Edition published by Wiley-VCH GmbH


moles adsorbed during charging cycles is about 52 mmol CO2 and 4.4 mmol O2 per kg of electrode active mass. To find the changes taking place on the electrodes when exposed to the CO2/O2/N2 gas mixture, we conducted in situ Raman spectroscopy experiments with a modified SSA cell (Figure S5). No additional peak except SiO2 vibrational modes (around 500 cm 1, 900 cm 1, 1100 cm 1 coming from the Quartz window), D band (~ 1350 cm 1), and G band (~ 1600 cm 1) was observed (Figure SS10), regardless the presence or direction ( 1 V and + 1 V) of the potential. The results show that the electrodes are stable at the conditions measured, but the measurements were not sensitive enough to reveal changes in the surface functional groups following charge and discharge.
Conclusion
Enhanced CO2 adsorption capacities and kinetics are observed when a 15 % CO2/85 % N2 gas mixture is replaced with a 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2 gas mixture. We report an 11 times higher CO2 adsorption capacity (~ 750 mmol kg 1) with coal-derived BPL electrodes using a 3 M MgBr2 electrolyte at 0.6 V, and a 4–5 times higher CO2 adsorption capacity with coal-derived BPL electrodes (320 mmol kg 1) and garlic roots-derived micro-mesoporous electrodes (~ 780 mmol kg 1) using a 3 M MgCl2 electrolyte at 1 V in the presence of O2. Coulombic efficiency, energy efficiency
and energy consumption improved significantly as the voltage window was systematically reduced from 1 V to 0.3 V, or when the voltage holding time was lowered from 60 min to 0 min, but at the expense of a decreased adsorption capacity. Small, partially reversible changes in O2 concentrations were observed during the charge-discharge cycles, indicating selectivity of CO2 over O2 at 0.5 V. Varying the oxygen concentrations (10 %, 15 %, 20 %) gave a similar energetic and adsorptive performance. The enhanced reversible CO2 adsorption in the presence of O2 can be attributed to an enhanced specific capacitance in the presence of O2.
Experimental
Materials
Coal-derived BPL 4×6 carbon (Calgon) and garlic roots (KV farms, Stroudsburg, PA, USA) were used as activated carbon sources. 60 % PTFE dispersion (Sigma Aldrich), conductive carbon black (VXCMAX22, Cabot Corporation), gluten (Hodgson Mill), ethanol (190 proof, Decon Labs), and DI water (18 MΩ) were used as binder, conductive agent, hydrophilic co-binder, and solvent, respectively. 3 M MgCl2 and 3 M MgBr2 were used as electrolyte solutions and filter paper (Whatman Grade 2, GE Healthcare Life Sciences) was used as a separator.
Figure 5. Performance metrics of SSA with garlic roots-derived activated carbon electrodes and a 3 M MgCl2 electrolyte, showing: (a) capacitance, adsorption capacity, energy consumption, and coulombic efficiency comparison at 1 V without O2 and at 1 V, 0.6 V, 0.5 V, 0.4 V and 0.3 V with O2, and (b) simultaneous measurement of CO2 and O2 concentration changes during charging and discharging of the electrodes at 0.5 V.
Angewandte Chemie
Research Article
Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202404881 (8 of 11) © 2024 The Author(s). Angewandte Chemie International Edition published by Wiley-VCH GmbH


Preparation of Activated Carbons
BPL 4×6 carbon was used as received without any further treatment. For the preparation of garlic roots-derived activated carbon, as-received garlic roots were washed several times with DI water and soaked in isopropyl alcohol overnight. The resulting sample was washed again with DI water, dried in the oven at 100 °C for 24 h, and pulverized to achieve a particle size of � 350 μm. 30 g of powdered garlic roots sample was uniformly mixed with 120 g of K2CO3 and transferred to a custom-made Ni boat. The sample was then transferred to a tube furnace and heated to 600 °C at 6 °C/min ramp rate. The temperature was maintained at 600 °C for 1 h, then increased to 800 °C at 6 °C/min ramp rate, maintained at 800 °C for 1 h, and allowed to cool to room temperature naturally. Ar gas was used at a flowrate of 50 sccm to maintain the inert atmosphere inside the tube. For air treatment, the sample was heated in the presence of air (20 sccm) to 420 °C at 6 °C/min ramp rate for 300 min. The resulting activated carbon sample was washed several times with 1 M HCl and DI water until the pH reached 7.0. The sample was dried in the oven at 100 °C for 24 h. The final yield of the sample was around 15 %. The resulting air oxidized garlic-rootsderived activated carbon was used to prepare the electrodes.
Electrodes Preparation and Supercapacitor Assembly
0.30 g of PTFE was added to 25 mL of ethanol. The solution was mixed and sonicated for 10 min to obtain a homogeneous mixture. 3.0 g of activated carbon, 0.37 g gluten, and 0.30 g conductive carbon black were added to the PTFE solution. The mixture was covered with Al foil and magnetically stirred at 60–65 °C for 2 h. The temperature was then increased to 80 °C for 30–45 min to evaporate the remaining solvent. The resulting dough was transferred onto a glass plate,, kneaded with a metal spatula, and rolled through a pasta rolling machine to prepare ~ 0.7 mm thick, 30 cm2 square shaped electrodes. The electrodes were placed in a vacuum oven at 100 °C and 25 mmHg for 12 h. The bottom electrode was soaked in 3 M MgBr2 or 3 M MgCl2 solution for 2 hours. A 36 cm2 filter paper was wetted with electrolyte and used as a separator. A 30 cm2 carbon cloth (AvCarb 1071 HCB) was used to cover the top electrode and served as a gas diffusion layer. The electrodes, separator, and gas diffusion layer were surrounded by an EPDM rubber gasket (9.5 cm×9.5 cm outer area, 8 cm×8 cm inside area, 0.29 cm thickness, Fuel cell store) and sandwiched between titanium grade 7 plates (13 cm×13 cm, 0.95 cm thick), which served as current collectors. The resulting assembly was pressed together by evenly tightening 16 set screws connecting the Ti plates using a torque wrench to 20 in.lb of torque.
Supercapacitive Swing Adsorption (SSA) Testing
A similar SSA setup as discussed previously was used (Scheme 1).[24] Briefly, a 15 % CO2/5 % O2/80 % N2 gas mixture passes through a mass flow controller adjusted to a flow rate of 5 sccm. The gas passes through a bubbler filled with electrolyte solution to moisten the gas mixture and avoid drying out of the electrodes during SSA experiments. The moistened gas mixture enters the SSA module from the center inlet port (1 mm in diameter) and flows radially through the gas diffusion layer inside the module. The gas exits from the outlet port at the corner of the top Ti plate, passes through a drying tube, and is then analyzed by a CO2 analyzer (Quantek Instruments, Model 906, Model 902P). The gas mixture was flown through the modules for 4–8 h without applying any bias to complete conventional CO2 adsorption to the electrodes and conventional CO2 absorption by the electrolyte. After that time, the concentration of the exiting gas attained a constant value of 15 % showing that conventional ad/absorption was complete. The module was then charged at a rate of 50 mA/g using different voltage
windows. The potential was held at the highest charging voltage for an additional time to allow for maximum saturation of the electrode with CO2. After that, the module was discharged to 0 V at 50 mA/g followed by a holding step to complete the desorption of CO2 gas from the electrode.
SSA Performance Metrics
Energetic Metrics
The SSA energetic metrics include the calculation of equivalent series resistance (ESR, Ω cm2), gravimetric capacitance (Cs, F g 1), charging time (tg, s), coulombic efficiency (ηc, %), energy efficiency (ηe, %), and energy loss (ΔE, J). These metrics were obtained from galvanostatic charge–discharge curves.

The discharge capacitances were calculated using the same discharging time in the equation Cs 1⁄4 4:I:tg
m:DV.
SSA Adsorptive Metrics
The SSA adsorptive metrics include the calculation of the number of moles of CO2 adsorbed during charging plus holding step (n avg., μmol), adsorption capacity with respect to mass (AC, mmol kg 1), area (AC, mmol m2), and volume (AC, mol.m3) of the gas-exposed electrode, adsorption rate (AR, μmol kg 1 s 1), productivity (P, mmol h 1 m 2), charge efficiency (CE, dimensionless), and energy consumption (EC, KJ mol 1).

EIS Measurements
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed at 0 V DC in the frequency range from 105 Hz to 10 3 Hz. Information about the solution resistance (Rs), charge transfer resistance (RCT), Warburg diffusion resistance (RD) and capacitance were extracted from the EIS data. The specific capacitance from EIS data calculated using the following relation:[31–33]
Cs 1⁄4 1
2p:f :Zimag
Here, Cs represent the specific capacitance. f is the frequency and Zimag is the imaginary impedance.
In situ Raman Characterization of the Electrodes
In situ Raman spectra were collected on a Horiba LabRam-HR Raman spectrometer using a 532 nm excitation wavelength laser source (Oxxius, filtered to 1.5 mW) and a thermoelectrically cooled Horiba Synapse BIDD scientific CCD camera detector. The laser was focused through a quartz window onto the top electrode as shown in Figure S5a, with a 5× objective (Olympus MPLN5X) while the spectrometer was used with a 500 nm grating and a 100 μm hole, resulting in a spectral resolution of ~1.7 cm 1. The 520.7 cm 1 band of a silicon wafer standard was used for calibration prior to spectral acquisition. Spectra was collected at several different voltages with and without oxygen in the gas mixture.
